\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Long-context language models place acute pressure on the key--value (KV) cache, which grows linearly with sequence length \cite{kwon-sosp2023, pope-mlsys2023}.
Two complementary responses---\emph{attention head pruning} \cite{voita-acl2019, michel-neurips2019} and \emph{KV cache eviction} \cite{snapkv-neurips2024, adakv-neurips2025}---can be deployed simultaneously as \emph{compound sparsity}, but the resulting quality degradation is often super-additive \cite{spark-aaai2026, slim-icml2025}. Recent evaluations confirm that reasoning capabilities degrade disproportionately under compound compression \cite{unicomp-2026}, and that per-dimension safe zones intersect to form a smaller joint safe region \cite{phase-transition-compression-2026}.

Prior work treats compound interaction magnitude as roughly constant across generation \cite{spark-aaai2026, unicomp-2026}, despite evidence that pruning sensitivity depends on representational phase \cite{decision-repr-transition-2026} and that no single sparse attention strategy dominates across generation stages \cite{sparse-frontier-2025}.
This assumption is problematic for reasoning models, whose generations alternate between broadly distributed attention (exploratory reasoning) and sharply concentrated attention (structured computation) \cite{thinkv-iclr2026}.
Phase-aware methods like ThinKV \cite{thinkv-iclr2026} apply different KV strategies per phase but without considering compound interaction, while importance-based eviction itself faces challenges from greedy bias \cite{greedy-bias-kvcache-2026}, deferred importance \cite{retentivekv-2026}, and temporal dynamics in long generations \cite{lethe-aaai2026}. These methods each optimize a single pruning axis; we characterize the interaction when multiple mechanisms are composed.
If compound severity varies across these phases, a uniform sparsity budget may be safe in one phase yet destructive in another.

What does compound interaction add beyond single-axis findings? HIES~\cite{hies-2025} characterizes score collapse; ThinKV~\cite{thinkv-iclr2026} introduces phase-aware eviction; \citet{sparse-frontier-2025} document strategy non-dominance across stages. Combining these insights qualitatively predicts phase-dependent compound degradation---but two quantitative patterns cannot be derived from single-axis analyses. First, the severity gradient follows a \emph{strictly monotonic dose-response} across sparsity levels (Jonckheere-Terpstra $z{=}33.7$, $p \ll 10^{-10}$), not merely a directional trend. Second, in DeepSeek a \emph{strategy ranking crossover} emerges at $s{=}0.25$---importance-based eviction simultaneously outperforms random in high-sparsity phases and underperforms in low-sparsity phases; Qwen shows consistent importance dominance without crossover, indicating model dependence. We report both the paired median difference $\Delta$ ($0.39 \to 8.48$) as the primary metric and the amplification ratio $G{=}7.5$--$79.8{\times}$ (importance) vs.\ $G \approx 1$ (random) as an auxiliary measure; $G$ is amplified by near-zero $\mathrm{II}_{\textit{high}}$ denominators, but $\Delta$---which involves no ratios---shows the same monotonic gradient (\S\ref{sec:results}).

We show that compound sparsity severity is strongly modulated by reasoning phase and eviction strategy.
Under importance-based KV cache eviction, the Interaction Index---a measure of super-additive degradation---concentrates in low-sparsity phases and is largely absent in high-sparsity phases.
On DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B (500 MATH-500 problems), the median phase difference rises from $0.39$ at $s{=}0.15$ to $8.48$ at $s{=}0.30$ (all Bonferroni-corrected $p \ll 10^{-10}$; Jonckheere-Terpstra $z{=}33.7$, $p \ll 10^{-10}$).
The pattern replicates on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct ($\Delta$: $0.07 \to 3.16$; all $p < 10^{-14}$); preliminary evidence from DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B (LlamaForCausalLM) suggests the phenomenon may extend beyond Qwen2 but at ${\sim}1/40$ the magnitude and with substantially weaker strategy contrast.
Random eviction develops a detectable but weak phase gradient only above $s \approx 0.20$ ($3$--$17{\times}$ smaller than importance-based where both strategies are significant, $s \geq 0.25$), confirming that the dominant gradient is an emergent phase-strategy interaction.

We present preliminary correlational evidence for \emph{importance discrimination collapse}---the degeneration of head importance scores toward uniformity under compound stress---as a contributing factor, with the \emph{structural specificity} of importance-based pruning (which selectively removes high-score heads) as a key differentiator from random pruning.

This work is a \textbf{diagnostic study}: we characterize a previously unknown interaction effect rather than proposing a mitigation method. Following the tradition of empirical analysis papers in NLP \cite{voita-acl2019, michel-neurips2019}, our contribution is establishing and quantifying the phenomenon of phase-modulated compound severity, providing measurement tools and diagnostic findings that inform future method design.
Our contributions:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
    \item We identify a \textbf{phase--strategy interaction}: importance-based eviction exhibits a severity gradient across reasoning phases that is $3$--$17{\times}$ larger than under random eviction where both strategies show significant phase gradients ($s \geq 0.25$) on MATH-500; the gradient direction is consistent on GSM8K but with task-modulated attenuation ($1.1$--$2.2{\times}$; \S\ref{sec:cross-benchmark}).\footnote{The full MATH-500 range including non-significant random conditions ($s \leq 0.20$, where random $\Delta$ CIs span zero) extends to $39{\times}$.}
    \item We show this gradient \textbf{increases monotonically with sparsity} and replicates across two Qwen2-architecture models (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct), with exploratory evidence from a LlamaForCausalLM model suggesting the phenomenon may extend beyond Qwen2 (\S\ref{sec:results}).
    \item We provide a \textbf{diagnostic analysis} revealing that aggregate score collapse (Gini) is necessary but not sufficient for severity amplification, pointing to structural specificity of pruned heads as the key differentiator (\S\ref{sec:analysis}).
\end{enumerate}
